# Equivalence of Definitions of Adjunction

**Conventions.** $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same objects as $\mathbf D$ (we write $D^{\mathrm{op}}$ for $D$ viewed in $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}$), and a morphism $f^{\mathrm{op}} : D_1^{\mathrm{op}} \to D_2^{\mathrm{op}}$ of $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}$ is exactly a morphism $f : D_2 \to D_1$ of $\mathbf D$, with $g^{\mathrm{op}} \circ f^{\mathrm{op}} = (f \circ g)^{\mathrm{op}}$. The product category $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}} \times \mathbf C$ has as objects the pairs $(D^{\mathrm{op}}, C)$ and as morphisms $(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1) \to (D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)$ the pairs $(f^{\mathrm{op}}, g)$ with $f^{\mathrm{op}} : D_1^{\mathrm{op}} \to D_2^{\mathrm{op}}$ in $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $g : C_1 \to C_2$ in $\mathbf C$; composition is componentwise. Local smallness of $\mathbf C, \mathbf D$ guarantees all hom-classes below are sets, so the functors below really land in $\mathbf{Set}$.

In both definitions $F$ and $G$ are the same kind of data (covariant functors $F:\mathbf D\to\mathbf C$, $G:\mathbf C\to\mathbf D$). So it suffices to show: for fixed $F,G$, a family $\alpha = \big(\alpha_{(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)}\big)$ indexed by objects of $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf C$ is a natural isomorphism $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(F-,-) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(-,G-)$ (Definition 1) if and only if it satisfies the conditions of Definition 2.

## Step 1: The two bifunctors explicitly

The hom bifunctor $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} : \mathbf C^{\mathrm{op}} \times \mathbf C \to \mathbf{Set}$ sends $(X^{\mathrm{op}}, Y)$ to $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(X,Y)$ and a morphism $(u^{\mathrm{op}}, g) : (X_1^{\mathrm{op}},Y_1) \to (X_2^{\mathrm{op}},Y_2)$ (so $u : X_2 \to X_1$, $g: Y_1 \to Y_2$) to the mapping $h \mapsto g \circ h \circ u$ from $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(X_1,Y_1)$ to $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(X_2,Y_2)$.

The hom bifunctor with left functor $F$ is the composite
$$H_1 := \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(F-,-) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} \circ (F^{\mathrm{op}} \times \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf C}) : \mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf C \to \mathbf{Set},$$
where $F^{\mathrm{op}}(f^{\mathrm{op}}) = (Ff)^{\mathrm{op}}$. Hence on objects $H_1(D^{\mathrm{op}},C) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD, C)$, and for $(f^{\mathrm{op}},g) : (D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)\to(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)$ (so $f : D_2\to D_1$ and $Ff : FD_2 \to FD_1$),
$$H_1(f^{\mathrm{op}},g) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(Ff^{\mathrm{op}}, g) : \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD_1,C_1)\to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD_2,C_2),\quad h \mapsto g\circ h\circ Ff .$$
(The composite is well typed: $Ff : FD_2\to FD_1$, $h : FD_1 \to C_1$, $g : C_1\to C_2$.)

Likewise the hom bifunctor with right functor $G$ is
$$H_2 := \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(-,G-) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}\circ(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}}\times G),$$
with $H_2(D^{\mathrm{op}},C) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D, GC)$ and
$$H_2(f^{\mathrm{op}},g) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(f^{\mathrm{op}}, Gg) : \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D_1,GC_1)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D_2,GC_2),\quad h\mapsto Gg\circ h\circ f .$$
(Well typed: $f: D_2\to D_1$, $h : D_1\to GC_1$, $Gg : GC_1\to GC_2$.)

These are precisely the mappings named $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(Ff^{\mathrm{op}},g)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(f^{\mathrm{op}},Gg)$ in Definition 2. (That $H_1,H_2$ are functors follows since they are composites of functors; it can also be checked directly: identities go to $h\mapsto h$, and for composable $(f_1^{\mathrm{op}},g_1)$, $(f_2^{\mathrm{op}},g_2)$ one has $g_2\circ(g_1\circ h\circ Ff_1)\circ Ff_2 = (g_2\circ g_1)\circ h\circ F(f_1\circ f_2)$, where $(f_2^{\mathrm{op}}\circ f_1^{\mathrm{op}}) = (f_1\circ f_2)^{\mathrm{op}}$; similarly for $H_2$.)

## Step 2: Isomorphisms in $\mathbf{Set}$ are bijections

A mapping $\phi : A\to B$ has a two-sided inverse $\psi$ ($\psi\circ\phi = \mathrm{id}_A$, $\phi\circ\psi=\mathrm{id}_B$) iff it is a bijection: a two-sided inverse forces injectivity (from $\psi\circ\phi=\mathrm{id}_A$) and surjectivity (from $\phi\circ\psi=\mathrm{id}_B$); conversely a bijection has its inverse mapping as two-sided inverse.

## Step 3: Natural isomorphisms are exactly natural transformations with bijective components

A natural isomorphism $\alpha : H_1\to H_2$ is a natural transformation having an inverse natural transformation $\beta : H_2\to H_1$ (i.e. $\beta\circ\alpha = \mathrm{id}_{H_1}$, $\alpha\circ\beta=\mathrm{id}_{H_2}$, composition being componentwise); equivalently, a natural transformation all of whose components are isomorphisms. We verify this equivalence so that either reading of the definition may be used.

- If $\beta$ is an inverse natural transformation, then componentwise $\beta_X\circ\alpha_X = \mathrm{id}$ and $\alpha_X\circ\beta_X=\mathrm{id}$, so every $\alpha_X$ is an isomorphism.
- Conversely, suppose $\alpha$ is natural and each $\alpha_X$ has inverse $\beta_X$. For any morphism $\varphi : X\to Y$ of $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf C$, naturality gives $\alpha_Y\circ H_1\varphi = H_2\varphi\circ\alpha_X$. Composing with $\beta_Y$ on the left and $\beta_X$ on the right:
$$H_1\varphi\circ\beta_X = \beta_Y\circ\alpha_Y\circ H_1\varphi\circ\beta_X = \beta_Y\circ H_2\varphi\circ\alpha_X\circ\beta_X = \beta_Y\circ H_2\varphi,$$
so $\beta$ is natural and is inverse to $\alpha$.

By Step 2, in $\mathbf{Set}$ "each component is an isomorphism" means "each component is a bijection".

## Step 4: Definition 1 $\Rightarrow$ Definition 2

Let $\alpha : H_1\to H_2$ be a natural isomorphism. Its components are mappings $\alpha_{(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)} : H_1(D^{\mathrm{op}},C) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD,C)\to H_2(D^{\mathrm{op}},C) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D,GC)$, one for each object $D^{\mathrm{op}}$ of $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $C$ of $\mathbf C$; by Steps 2–3 each is a bijection. Given $f^{\mathrm{op}}:D_1^{\mathrm{op}}\to D_2^{\mathrm{op}}$ in $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $g : C_1\to C_2$ in $\mathbf C$, the pair $(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)$ is a morphism $(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)\to(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)$ of $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf C$, and naturality of $\alpha$ at it reads, by Step 1,
$$\alpha_{(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)}\circ\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(Ff^{\mathrm{op}},g) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(f^{\mathrm{op}},Gg)\circ\alpha_{(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)},$$
which is exactly the commuting square of Definition 2. So $(F,G,\alpha)$ is an adjunction in the sense of Definition 2.

## Step 5: Definition 2 $\Rightarrow$ Definition 1

Let $(F,G,\alpha)$ satisfy Definition 2. Then $\alpha$ assigns to each object $(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)$ of $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf C$ a mapping $\alpha_{(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)} : H_1(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)\to H_2(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)$, i.e. a morphism in $\mathbf{Set}$ between the correct objects. Every morphism of $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf C$ from $(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)$ to $(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)$ is of the form $(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)$ with $f^{\mathrm{op}}:D_1^{\mathrm{op}}\to D_2^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $g:C_1\to C_2$, and for it the hypothesis of Definition 2 together with Step 1 gives
$$\alpha_{(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)}\circ H_1(f^{\mathrm{op}},g) = H_2(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)\circ\alpha_{(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)}.$$
Hence $\alpha$ is a natural transformation $H_1\to H_2$. Each component is a bijection, hence (Step 2) an isomorphism in $\mathbf{Set}$, so by Step 3 $\alpha$ is a natural isomorphism $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(F-,-)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(-,G-)$. Thus $(F,G,\alpha)$ is an adjunction in the sense of Definition 1.

Steps 4 and 5 together show the two definitions are equivalent. $\blacksquare$
